title: Couples Holding Hands
description:
# Couples Holding Hands

There are `n` couples sitting in `2n` seats arranged in a row. The people are represented by an integer array `row`, where `row[i]` is the ID of the person in seat `i`.

Partners have fixed ids `(0,1)`, `(2,3)`, `(4,5)`, and so on. Seats are paired too: indices `(0,1)` form the first pair, `(2,3)` the second. Each seat pair must hold one couple, in either order.

In one move, you may choose any two people and swap their seats. Return the minimum number of swaps needed so that every couple sits side by side.

## Example 1

**Input:** row = [0,2,1,3]

**Output:** 1

**Explanation:** Person `0` should sit next to person `1`. Swap people `2` and `1`, producing `[0,1,2,3]`.

## Example 2

**Input:** row = [3,2,0,1]

**Output:** 0

**Explanation:** Couples `(2,3)` and `(0,1)` are already adjacent. The order inside each pair does not matter.

## Constraints

* `2 <= row.length <= 60`
* `row.length` is even
* `0 <= row[i] < row.length`
* All values in `row` are unique

solutions.name: Position-Array Greedy Swap
solutions.description:
## Approach

Process the sofas from left to right. For each sofa, keep the left person fixed, compute that person's partner with `first ^ 1`, and use a position array to find the partner's current seat. If the partner is not already on the right seat of this sofa, swap the current right person with the partner.

## Key Insight

Once a sofa is fixed, later swaps never need to touch it again. Putting the correct partner beside the left person uses exactly one swap when the sofa is wrong, and no optimal solution can fix that sofa with fewer than one swap.

## Complexity Analysis

Building the position array takes O(n) time, and every sofa is processed once. Each swap and position update is O(1), so the total time is O(n). The position array uses O(n) space.

solutions.name: Union-Find on Couple IDs
solutions.description:
## Approach

Treat each couple ID, `person / 2`, as a node. Every sofa currently contains two people; union the two couple IDs represented on that sofa. If a connected component contains `s` couples, the sofas in that component are mixed together and need `s - 1` swaps.

## Key Insight

A swap inside one connected component can reduce that component's disorder by one couple. Components are independent, so the total answer is the number of couples minus the number of connected components.

## Complexity Analysis

There are `n` sofas and therefore O(n) union operations. With path compression and union by size, the total time is O(n * alpha(n)), and the parent and size arrays use O(n) space.

solutions.name: Couple Graph DFS Components
solutions.description:
## Approach

Build an undirected graph whose nodes are couple IDs. For every sofa, connect the two couple IDs sitting on that sofa. Then run depth-first search over this graph. A component with `s` couple nodes contributes `s - 1` swaps.

## Key Insight

A connected component captures exactly the couples whose members are interleaved across the same group of sofas. No swap outside that component is useful, and each internal swap can permanently place one couple.

## Complexity Analysis

The graph has `n` nodes and at most `2n` adjacency entries. Building it and running DFS are O(n) time. The adjacency lists, seen array, and recursion stack use O(n) space.

solutions.name: Sofa Graph Union-Find
solutions.description:
## Approach

Instead of making couples the nodes, make sofa indices the nodes. Scan every person and remember the first sofa where each couple appears. When the second member of that couple is found, union the two sofas containing that couple. The number of swaps is the number of sofas minus the number of sofa components.

## Key Insight

If a couple is split across two sofas, those sofas belong to the same repair component. A component of `s` sofas can be solved in `s - 1` swaps, regardless of which couple is used to connect the sofas.

## Complexity Analysis

The scan is O(n), with at most one union per couple. Union-find gives O(n * alpha(n)) total time. The first-sofa, parent, and size arrays use O(n) space.

solutions.name: Compact BFS over Couple Cycles
solutions.description:
## Approach

The couple graph has very small degree: every misplaced couple can touch at most two sofas. Store the graph in fixed two-slot neighbor arrays, then use a queue to breadth-first-search each component and add `componentSize - 1` to the answer.

## Key Insight

This is the same component formula as the graph proof, but it avoids recursive DFS and avoids allocating many tiny adjacency lists. It is useful when teaching the cycle structure hidden inside the seating arrangement.

## Complexity Analysis

Each sofa contributes at most two directed neighbor entries, and each couple is enqueued once. Time is O(n), and the fixed neighbor arrays plus queue use O(n) space.
